newsitem.title: UK: LME markets end mostly lower, copper sickly.
newsitem.headline: LME markets end mostly lower, copper sickly.

text.p: LME base metal prices came under late pressure and veered lower, with copper and aluminium ending an erratic day around their lows.

Traders said the trend was not uniform, as nickel bounced on news of a strike vote at Canada's Falconbridge and zinc built on earlier support. However, overall market sentiment seemed to be sickening, they said.
"Copper and aluminium are getting near levels where people want to sell - it does not look too good at the moment," one trader said.
Copper lurched lower when the market decisively broke under intermediate support around $2,375/2,380, with prices speedily retreating to the mid-$2,360s.
Traders said the market is paying no attention to the strike at Portugal's Neves Corvo, even though there is a total stoppage and the mine has supplies for only a week.
Instead, general liquidation and fresh selling is bearing down on the market against a background of rising stocks and expectations of some hefty increases in the next few weeks.
Inventories are seen rising in the U.S., Europe, and the Far East, attracted by the high spot premiums.
"The July backwardation is the only thing that is holding it up really - people are looking to sell it now because they see production rising faster than consumption," another trader said.
Last three months business was at $2,368 a tonne, down $31 from Monday's kerb. A break under $2,355 could usher in further significant falls.

Meanwhile, nickel prices reversed direction during the late kerb, responding to news that unionized workers at Falconbridge's Sudbury facility voted for a strike mandate ahead of an August 1 contract expiry.
Traders noted that only recently Inco workers at Sudbury were on strike for four weeks.
Final business was at $6,935, up $135 from the earlier low and a $75 gain from overnight.
Zinc was also steadier, rebounding from downside support below $1,450 to close at $1,460, a $4 gain.
However, aluminium was depressed by copper, and skidded down to $1,565, down $22, with trade support unable to stave off fund sales.
Lead and tin traded quietly and both sagged, albeit in narrow ranges. Lead was $5 easier at $649, while tin shed $10 to $5,540.
Alloy was quoted at a softer $1,425/35 a tonne.
